newsitem.title: UK: Wet Brent weaker, weighed down by surplus barrels.
newsitem.headline: Wet Brent weaker, weighed down by surplus barrels.

text.p: North Sea physical and cash markets weakened again on Tuesday, with a wet Brent deal struck at a new recent low of July -70 cents a barrel, traders said.
The dated Brent cargo loading 17-19 June was done 8 cents lower than one due on the same dates which traded on Monday, and 21 below a deal struck for a June 16-19 cargo done on Friday.
The trading house which kept two cargoes from the paper chains on Monday was believed to be the seller and was thought to be trying to reoffer the Monday cargoes.

Short-dated swaps weakened sharply as news of the physical deal hit the market. CFDs for next week (June 16-20) dropped to talk around August Brent -77 cents, and the next week (June 23-27) at August -68 cents.
"It's falling sharply, the front end has really taken a pounding," said one paper trader. No paper deals were heard done, however.
The June/July intermonth spread was offered at -35 cents, but bids were much lower. July/August held at the level traded in the U.S. aftermarket at around -30/-28 cents.
Outright July paper recovered slightly from Monday's losses, trading at $17.78 and $17.73 a barrel in morning business.
Wet Brent's weakness stemmed from the narrow transatlantic arbitrage window, which has trapped crude in Europe, traders said.
The premium for July NYMEX crude over July Brent has slipped to just $1, 50 cents off the differential North Sea sellers generally require for profitable transatlantic sales.
Just one Brent cargo, deferred from June 14-16 to 25-27, was due to turn wet on Tuesday.

Other North Sea grades have also slipped, with June barrels still abundant. A Statfjord traded at Dated Brent plus a cent on Monday, three cents off a deal on Friday, and 24 cents down on a deal earlier last week.
Other trades were heard to have been conducted on a private and confidential basis. Those sellers with storage were building stocks, traders said.
In the Mediterranean, one trader reported a Urals done on Friday at a firmer $1.18 discount to benchmark Dated Brent but others said the value looked too high.
"I doubt that. I just don't see it. I mean it's possible but there are other cargoes available," one said. "I'd put the market closer to the upper 20s."
Traders said available Urals cargoes comprised at least two one million barrel stems including a 19-20 loader and a 23-24 loader and two 80,000 tonners including a 22-23 loader and a 26-27 loader.

"What is clear is that this is a favourable moment to sell," said one trader. "There has been a lot of noise about this -$1.18 deal and we all know the Iraqis are coming up again - there is even talk that someone is already looking for a (June) 21-22 loader for a Kirkuk."
"And the closer we get to the end of June the closer we get to the July Russian programmes.
"Although people say they don't expect Kirkuk until July, this is just speculation at the end of the day. The truth is still out there waiting to be discovered, just like the X-Files."
In West Africans, Qua Iboe continued to be assessed unchanged at a premium in the mid-30s over Dated Brent, with Bonny Light in the low to mid-40s.

One Asian trader was heard picking up an Odudu at a discount of around five cents to Dated on Monday and traders also reported talk that two Osos loading in the second and third decade had changed hands but there were no immediate details.
